lines.text: Golden pagodas, great kingdoms of the Irrawaddy, British rule and a long struggle between the army and the people. This is the story of Myanmar.
It begins more than two thousand years ago, with the Pyu, whose Buddhist cities rose along the Irrawaddy River.
On a hill in what is now Yangon rose the Shwedagon, a great golden stupa that is still the most sacred site in the land.
In the ninth century Bagan grew on the dry plains of the Irrawaddy. Thousands of its temples and pagodas still stand today.
From Bagan, the Pagan Kingdom became the first to unite the land, filling its capital with temples.
Its founding king was Anawrahta, who in the eleventh century built Pagan into an empire.
After Pagan fell to Mongol attacks, a new power rose centuries later: the Toungoo dynasty.
Its king Bayinnaung conquered his neighbours and built the largest empire in the history of South East Asia.
In 1752 the Konbaung kings came to power. They would be the last royal dynasty of Burma.
Three years later the Konbaung founder took a small town on the delta and named it Yangon. It would become the country's largest city.
From 1824 Britain fought three wars against the Burmese kings, and by 1885 it held the whole country.
In between, in 1857, King Mindon founded Mandalay, the last royal capital before the British came.
U Thant, born in 1909, would rise to lead the United Nations as its Secretary-General.
Aung San led the fight for independence and won its terms from Britain in 1947. Months before freedom came, he was assassinated.
During the Second World War, Burma became a battlefield, as Japanese armies fought British, Indian and Chinese forces from 1942 to 1945.
His daughter, Aung San Suu Kyi, was born in 1945. She would lead the fight for democracy and spend many years under house arrest.
In January 1948 Burma became independent. But its many peoples and its army would struggle for decades over who ruled.
Min Aung Hlaing, born in 1956, would rise to command the army and seize power for himself.
In 1988, after decades of army rule, students and monks rose up in the 8888 Uprising. The army crushed it.
In 2005 the generals moved the government to Naypyidaw, a new capital built in secret in the jungle.
In 2008 Cyclone Nargis struck the delta, killing some hundred and forty thousand people.
From 2016 the army turned on the Rohingya, a Muslim minority. Their villages burned, and hundreds of thousands fled.
In February 2021 the army seized power again, ending a decade of partial democracy.
Protest turned to resistance, and the coup led to a civil war that still divides the country.
Then in March 2025 a powerful earthquake struck near Mandalay, felt as far away as Bangkok.
From the temples of Bagan to a land at war, Myanmar's people still wait for peace.
